roots.value: I'm rebuilding the rear wheel on my gravel bike with a new rim and the old hub. Where do I even start?

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Start by removing the tire, tube and rim strip, then clamp the hub in a truing stand so the axle spins freely. Check the rim for flat spots and dents before you lace anything.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Sort the spokes into two groups. The drive-side spokes are shorter and pull from the right flange, while the non-drive-side spokes are longer. Mixing them up is the most common lacing mistake.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Lace the first set of spokes loosely so each nipple has about four threads showing. Cross each spoke over three others and weave the last crossing under the neighbouring spoke for clearance.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Add a drop of light oil to each spoke thread. This prevents the nipples from seizing and makes later adjustments much easier on a wheel that sees wet roads.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Okay, lacing is done. How do I true it?

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Work around the wheel in quarter turns. Lateral true comes first, then radial true, then dish. Resist the urge to chase one wobble with a single big adjustment because it moves the neighbours too.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Use a tensiometer at the end of each pass. Even tension matters more than hitting a number, and a spread of more than 15 percent between spokes is the usual cause of a wheel going out of true after the first ride.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Stress relieve by squeezing pairs of spokes together with gloved hands, then re-check the true. You will hear small pings as the nipples settle, which is normal.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Target drive-side spoke tension is 110 kgf for this rim, and the non-drive side will land near 70 kgf once the wheel is dished correctly. Do not exceed the rim manufacturer's limit.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: If a single spoke keeps losing tension, check the nipple seat for a burr and the spoke bed for a crack. Replacing one spoke is far cheaper than rebuilding the wheel after a failure on the road.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Now I'm mounting it. Do I need a torque wrench for the axle?

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Yes. Over-tightening can crush the bearings and under-tightening lets the cassette body wobble. Before you refit the wheel, clean the dropout faces and add a thin film of grease to the axle threads.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Fit the thru axle through the frame and hub, thread it in by hand until it seats, and only then bring the torque wrench to the fastener. Pull smoothly instead of jerking the handle.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Keep your hand near the head of the wrench, wipe off any excess grease so grit does not stick, and confirm the brake rotor sits centred between the pads on both sides of the caliper.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Spin the wheel to check that nothing rubs, and confirm the quick release lever on the disc side does not point into the rotor before you ride away. Take your time with this step and keep the work area clean, because small bits of grit on the threads or the seating faces are the usual reason a fastener never feels quite right. Work in good light, keep a rag nearby, and recheck each setting once more before moving on. roots.value: I also want to run tubeless. Any sealant tips?

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Tubeless works well on gravel. Use tape that is two millimetres wider than the rim channel and press it down firmly with a rag so no air can pass under it.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Seat the tire with a floor pump that has a booster chamber or a compressor. If the bead refuses to seat, remove the valve core to let more air through for the first rush.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Spin the wheel in all positions after inflating so the sealant coats the whole bead, and ride gently for the first few kilometres. roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Q: How long should the sealant cure before riding?

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Top up the sealant every four to six months and carry a tire plug kit for punctures that do not seal.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Last thing: how often should I check the wheel afterwards?

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Check the true and the spoke tension after the first ride, again after the first 100 km, and then at every service. A wheel that stays quiet and straight through the first month is usually stable for years.

roots.name: Conversation
roots.value: Listen for ticking from the hub or spokes; most noises are dry nipples or a loose cassette lockring, both of which take only minutes to fix.
